queries.query: the soul's ascent through the heavens to the divine

passages.title: Daqāʾiq al-Ḥaqāʾiq Or. 7008
passages.quote: the gates of heaven are opened for them, and angels from every heaven accompany it until they reach the seventh heaven
passages.why: The believer's soul at death is carried up by angels heaven by heaven to the seventh heaven and God's decree; the disbeliever's soul finds the gate shut.

passages.title: The Taoist Canon
passages.quote: the soul ascends to the Nine Heavens and merges with the Truth of the Dao
passages.why: Lingbao scripture: reciting it makes the spirit fly, the soul ascend the Nine Heavens, transcend the Three Realms and fly up to Highest Purity.

passages.title: The Apocalypse of Abraham
passages.quote: describes how the prophet was taken by an angel through the seven heavens, and what he saw there
passages.why: Summary of the Vision of Isaiah: the visionary is led by an angel through seven heavens to behold the Great Glory.

passages.title: On the Art of the Kabbalah
passages.quote: unless one ascends by degrees and ladders, which indeed, as you are accustomed to speak, [are] like the Homeric chain
passages.why: Reuchlin: the highest good, God, is reached only by ascending by degrees, Jacob's ladder stretched through the planetary orbs.

passages.title: Elijah with the Teachings of the Talmud and the Rabbis
passages.quote: He was so worthy that his soul ascended every night to the High School
passages.why: Report from Emek ha-Melekh of Luria's soul ascending nightly, escorted by angels, to the heavenly academy.

passages.title: The Republic
passages.quote: they commanded the just to Socrates, Glaucon. proceed to the right and upward through the heaven
passages.why: Myth of Er: judged souls of the just are sent upward through the opening in heaven.

passages.title: Astronomicon
passages.quote: Is it a matter of doubt that a god dwells within our breast? And that our souls return to heaven and come from heaven?
passages.why: Manilius: the mind surveys the cosmos and approaches the stars; souls come from and return to heaven.

passages.title: Monument of Ancient Christianity
passages.quote: so are such people already beforehand caught up and captivated into that world, and they behold everything that is glorious and wondrous there
passages.why: Macarian homily: the purified are already caught up into the heavenly world by stages and behold Christ's glory.

passages.title: The Ideal Shadow of Universal Wisdom
passages.quote: ascends to the SUPREME to consider there the HIGHEST MYSTERIES OF THE THEOLOGICAL, or DIVINE WORLD
passages.why: The soaring spirit rises region by region from created things to the supreme divine world.

queries.reader_notes: Pool windows miss the classic loci (Poimandres, Dream of Scipio descent/ascent chapter, mi'raj narratives, Ascension of Isaiah vision text itself; only its introduction is in the pool). i=181 is an editor's summary of a Jewish-Christian apocalypse. Nothing substantive found in hindu-indic, buddhist, zoroastrian for a soul's ascent through heavens.

queries.query: prima materia: the first matter from which all things are made

passages.title: On the Hyleal Chaos
passages.quote: entering into the Hyleal, that is, Pri-material watery CHAOS created at the first beginning of the World, sanctifying and also impregnating it
passages.why: Khunrath: Nature is a divine fire-spirit entering the hyleal, primaterial watery chaos from which the whole great world is built.

passages.title: Theatrum Chemicum Volumen Secundum
passages.quote: From one confused mass were created all things that now exist. This one principle can serve to declare the matter of our blessed stone.
passages.why: Ripley's axioms: God made all things from one confused chaos-mass, which is the key to the matter of the stone.

passages.title: Theatrum Chemicum Volumen Secundum
passages.quote: is a universal thing, enclosing within itself everything we work upon; from its belly the ingenious craftsman must draw out his matter, form, Heaven, and the Elements
passages.why: The chemical Chaos as the first and universal matter enclosing everything, from which the artist draws matter, form and elements.

passages.title: Two Books Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World
passages.quote: he himself created the primary matter, which he defines as the "receiver" and "nurse" of becoming
passages.why: Philoponus on the Timaeus: the Demiurge makes the primary matter, whose whole being is to be the receiver of becoming.

passages.title: Two Books Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World
passages.quote: it must necessarily be the ultimate substrate of natural things and the primary matter
passages.why: Philoponus argues what the immutable, quality-less ultimate substrate (primary matter) of natural bodies is.

passages.title: Theology of Aristotle
passages.quote: that the rational soul forms the first matter because of the power sent into it by the marvelous intellect
passages.why: Theology of Aristotle: the world consists of matter and form; first matter is formed by soul through intellect from the First Being.

passages.title: Confucian Cosmogony
passages.quote: is made from the same primordial Air as Heaven or Shang-te and Man, and the same inherent Principle
passages.why: Zhu Xi (in the translator's notes): every being down to an insect is made from one primordial Air (qi) animated by Principle.

passages.title: Confucian Cosmogony
passages.quote: the Infinite Primordial Air in which this Principle is inherent, is the material portion of Unity
passages.why: The primordial Air is the material portion of the Great One, which divides into the parts of the universe.

passages.title: The Bhagvat-Geeta, or Dialogues of Kreeshna and Arjoon
passages.quote: In it I place my seed original: "fœtus" , and from it comes the production of all nature. The great Brahm is the womb of all those various forms
passages.why: Gita 14: the great Brahm (prakriti) is the womb into which Krishna casts the seed and from which all forms are produced.

queries.reader_notes: Christian: only one-sentence mentions (Llull Ars Magna i=7738; Boehme's Mysterium Magnum pages are table captions) - left out. Jewish-kabbalistic: only passing hyle/tohu mentions. Duhem (shelf 'other', i=10656-10668) has a whole chapter on prime matter in Arabic Neoplatonism but is a modern history, not labelled. Samkhya window (i=5080-5119) is on liberation, not on prakriti as root-matter. Chinese pages are a 19th-c. translator's notes on Zhu Xi.

queries.query: emptiness: things have no fixed nature of their own

passages.title: Compendium of the Five Lamps
passages.quote: All things are originally empty, and because emptiness itself is empty, we call that state Stillness.
passages.why: Chan dialogue: all things are originally empty and emptiness itself is empty, so there is nothing to quiet.

passages.title: Kanjur 'Bum Cha
passages.quote: all phenomena are like a dream; in them, there is no one who teaches, no one who hears, and no one who understands
passages.why: Prajnaparamita: Subhuti teaches that all phenomena are like emanations and dreams, with no teacher, hearer or understander.

passages.title: The Religion of the Samurai: A Study of Zen Philosophy
passages.quote: if all phenomena are flowing and changing, there could be no constant reality underlying them. It therefore follows that all things in the universe are empty and unreal.
passages.why: Exposition of no-atman and unreality: since everything is transient there is no constant reality underlying things.

passages.title: The Compendium of Shiva
passages.quote: Therefore, these material things do not truly exist; only the great and glorious One that illuminates them exists.
passages.why: Shiva Samhita: distinctions are only names; material things are unreal reflections, only the One exists.

passages.title: The Bhagvat-Geeta, or Dialogues of Kreeshna and Arjoon
passages.quote: Something that is merely imaginary has no real existence, while that which is true can never cease to exist.
passages.why: Gita 2: sensations and bodies come and go and have no real existence; only the indestructible spirit is real.

passages.title: Books and Writings, Together with His Holy Miraculous Life
passages.quote: but not the creatures / who are not in themselves / but in God / for he is the life / the essence / and the working of all creatures / but we are nothing / except only in him
passages.why: Suso: only God is a constant being in himself; creatures have no being in themselves and are nothing except in him.

queries.reader_notes: Buddhist shelf is rich (also i=5065, 4602, 1841, 4969-4973 Prajnaparamita lists of emptinesses). Outside Buddhism the idea appears only as analogues: Vedantic unreality of the world (hindu) and the creature's nothingness apart from God (christian). Daoist pages (Zhuangzi commentary i=3245-3260, Liezi i=3582) speak of non-being/relativity but only in fragments or translator's gloss - left out. Nothing in greek-roman, jewish, islamic (Ghazali i=2991 is about doubt, not emptiness).

queries.query: what makes a human life go well; the highest good and true flourishing for a person

passages.title: On Duties
passages.quote: Those who place the highest good in virtue do well, but this very virtue produces and maintains friendship, and friendship cannot exist in any way without virtue.
passages.why: Cicero weighs candidates for the best thing in life (wealth, health, power, pleasure) and sides with those who place the highest good in virtue, with friendship.

passages.title: On the Nature of the Gods and Other Philosophical Works
passages.quote: to which justice is conjoined, and the remaining virtues from which a happy life exists, equal and similar to the gods
passages.why: Stoic speaker: knowledge of the heavens yields piety, justice and the virtues, from which comes a happy life like the gods'.

passages.title: On Duties
passages.quote: I suppose in him who has such a possession that he is easily content for living liberally. Who seeks nothing, desires nothing
passages.why: Stoic paradox that only the wise man is rich: true wealth is contentment needing nothing.

passages.title: The Consolation of Philosophy
passages.quote: the entire intention of the human will, which is driven by various pursuits, hastens toward happiness
passages.why: Boethius with commentary: every human will tends to happiness, happiness is the Good itself (summum bonum), attained only by the good.

passages.title: Aquinas Ethicus: Or, The Moral Teaching of St. Thomas
passages.quote: Now, the first element of happiness is perfection. Since happiness is the perfect good, it includes excellence or brilliance
passages.why: Aquinas: happiness is the perfect good with three elements (perfection, sufficiency, delight) that the vices counterfeit.

passages.title: al-Fuṣūl al-ḥikmīya, by al-Fārābī (d. 950)
passages.quote: he then learns the highest perfection that man acquired from the First. That perfection is happiness.
passages.why: Al-Farabi: man's highest perfection received from the First is happiness; wisdom gives the goal, practical discernment the means.

passages.title: On the Perfect State (Kitab Ara' Ahl al-Madina al-Fadila)
passages.quote: becomes stronger, better, and more complete, until it reaches a threshold of perfection where it becomes independent of matter
passages.why: Al-Farabi: the actions through which happiness is attained perfect the soul by habituation until it is independent of matter.

passages.title: Taoist Texts: Ethical, Political, and Speculative
passages.quote: Thus, he does not regard physical comfort as true happiness, nor penury as pitiable, nor an honourable position as one of tranquillity
passages.why: Daoist portrait of the perfected man: he prizes neither wealth nor fame and does not take comfort for true happiness.

passages.title: Four Books of Confucius - Analects, Great Learning, Doctrine of Mean, Mencius
passages.quote: "There is no greater delight than to be conscious of sincerity original: "誠" on self-examination.
passages.why: Mencius: the greatest delight is sincerity found on self-examination; perfect virtue is approached through reciprocity.

passages.title: Aṅguttara-Nikāya (Pali Text)
passages.quote: When there is contentment, friend, this happiness is to be expected: whether walking, one finds happiness and ease
passages.why: Anguttara: in this teaching discontent is suffering and contentment is happiness in every posture and place.

passages.title: The Householder's Dharma (Ratnakaranda-Sravakachara)
passages.quote: Which frees souls from the pain and misery of embodied existence and installs them in supreme bliss, that excellent karma -destroying dharma
passages.why: Jain householder's manual: the dharma of right faith, knowledge and conduct frees from misery and installs the soul in supreme bliss.

passages.title: On the Art of the Kabbalah
passages.quote: But the beatitude of the future is the apprehension of the highest good, above which there is no good, and from which is all goodness
passages.why: Reuchlin's Jewish speaker: present happiness is tranquillity of soul; future beatitude is apprehending the highest good, God.

queries.reader_notes: The 'Nicomachean Ethics' window (i=2640-2679) is actually Politics II text (property, community of goods), so no eudaimonia passage there. i=5245 is Jain (shelved hindu-indic). i=5109 Samkhya defines the Supreme Good as permanent prevention of pain, one sentence only - left out.

queries.query: the annihilation of the self in union with the divine

passages.title: Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn (Revival of the Religious Sciences)
passages.quote: Love is not valid until one departs from seeing the love itself to seeing the Beloved, through the annihilation of the knowledge of love
passages.why: Ghazali cites Sufi sayings: the lover is annihilated from his own love, the Beloved's attributes replace the lover's (I become his hearing and sight).

passages.title: مثنوی معنوی (Masnavī-yi Maʻnavī), Books 1-2
passages.quote: Because he walks into the light of witnessing, | He becomes, like a moth, annihilated in existence.
passages.why: Rumi: the man of Truth burns his existence like a moth in the light of witnessing, loving death to self.

passages.title: Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn (Revival of the Religious Sciences)
passages.quote: occurs in the station of persistence after passing through the threshold of annihilation
passages.why: Ghazali: intimacy with and awe of the Essence belong to the station of persistence (baqa) after annihilation (fana), with everything other than God severed.

passages.title: Books and Writings, Together with His Holy Miraculous Life
passages.quote: that we may thus arrive at the knowledge of our nothingness / so that we may be sunk / and swallowed up into the Divine Essence
passages.why: Suso sermon: one must die and become nothing (non sum) in order to be sunk and swallowed up into the divine essence.

passages.title: Handbook, or Short Instruction
passages.quote: Grant, LORD, that I may let go of myself, lose myself to myself, and become nothing; so that You remain everything in me
passages.why: Weigel's prayer of Gelassenheit: to let go of and lose oneself and become nothing so that God is all in the soul.

passages.title: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy
passages.quote: when its natural subsistence—that is, the primary notion—is absorbed by a greater abyss of light; it is no longer guided by its own light
passages.why: Dialogue: a creature perfectly united to God no longer subsists through itself but through God, as starlight is absorbed in the sun; nothing positive is destroyed.

passages.title: On the Harmony of the World
passages.quote: This transformation occurs through a departure of the mind and a certain ecstasy, Hebrews which the Hebrews call the death of the kiss
passages.why: Zorzi on the Hebrews' 'death of the kiss': in ecstasy the man dies to the body and the spirit is transformed into God.

passages.title: Composite manuscript: fragments of commentaries on the Torah and on the Song of Songs (Gaster Hebrew MS 1380)
passages.quote: My existence is annihilation, and in my annihilation, you exist.
passages.why: Quoted verse of a philosopher-poet: the heart addresses the One who fills every vessel; my existence is annihilation and in it You exist.

passages.title: Essence of Pomegranates
passages.quote: it becomes one with the perceiver. This is the secret of true devekut cleaving/attachment to the Divine which the prophets and the pious achieve
passages.why: Devekut explained: what the thinking soul perceives becomes one with it; this cleaving is the crown of the righteous.

passages.title: A History of Indian Philosophy, Volume 1
passages.quote: After this, the self that has become Brahman is no longer perceived; having emerged from all states of being, it has no remaining sign.
passages.why: Caraka quoted: in final renunciation consciousness ends and the self become Brahman is no longer perceived, a state like annihilation.

passages.title: A Series of Lessons in Gnani Yoga
passages.quote: It would have known that instead of being a tiny, insignificant dewdrop, it was a part of the Mighty Ocean—in fact, that its Real Self was that Ocean itself.
passages.why: Modern Jnana-yoga lesson: the dewdrop loses the illusion of separateness and glides into the ocean that is its real Self.

passages.title: The Compendium of Shiva
passages.quote: The individual soul is absorbed back into the source when the experience of its actions comes to an end.
passages.why: Shiva Samhita: when karma is exhausted the jiva is absorbed into the Supreme Brahman.

queries.reader_notes: i=1308 (van Helmont dialogue, shelved jewish-kabbalistic) is a Christian-Platonist argument, labelled christian. i=327 is the Christian kabbalist Zorzi reporting the Hebrew mors osculi. i=2235 is a Judeo-Arabic manuscript quoting a Sufi-style verse. i=6355 is a 1907 Western 'Yogi Ramacharaka' text. Buddhist nirvana pages are not union with a divine and were left out; Daoist self-forgetting not found in a substantive passage. Other good Christian pages: i=8222, 8210 (Suso), 2938 (Eckhart).

queries.query: spirits that stand between gods and humans

passages.title: On the Mysteries
passages.quote: about each one of the Gods there is an uncountable multitude of demons. And elsewhere: "Each God leads first the demons, then indeed particular souls."
passages.why: Notes on Iamblichus citing Proclus: each god commands an order of daemons, who stand between gods and particular souls and join souls to their leaders.

passages.title: On the Mysteries
passages.quote: According to the Egyptians, each person's own Daemon is attached to them at the hour of birth.
passages.why: Discussion of the personal daemon assigned as leader of the soul in this life and its rank among mundane daemons.

passages.title: The Republic
passages.quote: which they had chosen, to be the watcher over his life and the fulfiller E of his choices
passages.why: Myth of Er: Lachesis sends with each soul its daimon as guardian of the life and fulfiller of its choice.

passages.title: Summa Theologica
passages.quote: But angels are intermediate between God and humans, as they participate more in the perfection of divine goodness than humans do.
passages.why: Aquinas: by the Dionysian order the lowest are reached through intermediates, so divine revelation comes to humans through angels.

passages.title: On the Art of the Kabbalah
passages.quote: if we have applied our study to the angels, that we may be joined to God also through the angels by the ineffable Tetragrammaton
passages.why: Reuchlin: the seventy-two angels of the Name are the way back to God; all is done by God through the angels, not by angels themselves.

passages.title: On the Art of the Kabbalah
passages.quote: which they rejoice in by the name of angels when they descend to these lowest things, since they are the messengers of the King of kings
passages.why: Reuchlin: supercelestial 'gods of gods' come into our world only when sent, as angels, messengers of the King of kings, kindly toward us.

passages.title: Sphinx Mystagoga
passages.quote: certain natures were to be found midway between those Gods and men, which they called Angels, Demons, or Genii
passages.why: Kircher on Egyptian (Hermetic) belief in Genii midway between the celestial gods and men, source of oracles.

passages.title: Vedic Hymns Part Two
passages.quote: thou goest for us today as a messenger, thou who art born between the two races between humans and gods
passages.why: Rigveda hymn: Agni, born between the two races, goes as messenger between gods and tribes of men and brings the gods to the sacrifice.

passages.title: Theology of Aristotle
passages.quote: And that He illuminates the Intelligences, and through them as mediums, the Intellect; and through the Intellect indeed as a medium, the universal and celestial Soul.
passages.why: Theology of Aristotle: God acts on the lower world through a chain of mediating Intelligences, Intellect and Soul.

queries.reader_notes: Greek shelf is the core (Iamblichus notes, Republic X). i=9180 states the doctrine only in the page's last sentence (the continuation, i=9182, is on oracles and genii in statues). i=1942 is intermediary intelligences rather than spirits proper - weakest fit. Agni (i=6162) is a god acting as go-between. Nothing substantive in chinese, buddhist, zoroastrian (only passing 'messenger angel' at i=7481).

queries.query: the human being as a small copy of the whole universe

passages.title: Astrologie theologized
passages.quote: that creature was usually most fitly called the Microcosm, that is, the little or lesser world
passages.why: Weigel: Adam was made from a mass drawn from every part of the world's frame, so man is one and the same with the great world and is called microcosm.

passages.title: Handbook, or Short Instruction
passages.quote: the microcosm, that is, the little world / because he carries the great world within him / and is carried and fed by the great one
passages.why: Weigel: the great world with its creatures became the human, who is called microcosm because he carries the great world within him.

passages.title: On the Art of the Kabbalah
passages.quote: And since man is made as a certain image of this world, whence he is called a microcosmos small world , he receives in many respects worldly names
passages.why: Reuchlin: man is an image of the world (microcosmos), so his parts take cosmic names - mind is called God, etc.

passages.title: The Compendium of Shiva
passages.quote: Within this body exists Mount Meru, surrounded by the seven islands; there are rivers, oceans, mountains, fields, and the guardians of those fields.
passages.why: Shiva Samhita ch. II 'The Microcosm': the body (brahmanda) contains Meru, the islands, seas, sun and moon; who knows this is a yogi.

passages.title: Confucian Cosmogony
passages.quote: These two souls are precisely the same in the Kosmos and in Man, and hence the former is styled a Great Man, and the latter a microcosm
passages.why: Notes on Zhu Xi: the cosmos is a Great Man (Heaven the head, Earth the feet, sun and moon the eyes) and man a little Heaven.

passages.title: The Taoist Canon
passages.quote: The Brahma-Qi original: "Fanqi"; primordial, pure celestial energy. becomes the body, and through the transformation of Spirit and Qi, the Three Realms are naturally formed.
passages.why: Daoist scripture: the cosmic formation of heaven and underworld from spirit and qi is repeated inside the body (section headed internal microcosm).

passages.title: Astronomicon
passages.quote: If humans can possess the world itself within them? Each person is a miniature example of God, an image in small proportions.
passages.why: Manilius: man can know the world because he holds the world within him and is a small-scale image of the divine cosmos.

passages.title: Sacred and Truly Christian Philosophy, or Cosmic Meteorology
passages.quote: or man, the entire "fleshy earth" is affected by stupor, the loss of sensation and motion, and by chilling
passages.why: Fludd: each meteorological process of the macrocosm (frost, congelation) has its counterpart in the microcosm, man's fleshy earth.

passages.title: The Religion of the Samurai: A Study of Zen Philosophy
passages.quote: This life or living principle in the microcosmos is identical with that of the macrocosmos, and the Universal Life of the macrocosmos is the common source of all lives.
passages.why: Zen exposition: the life within each of us is identical with the universal life of the macrocosm (Buddha-nature).

queries.reader_notes: Hermetic shelf: the word microcosm is everywhere (Agrippa's scale tables, Khunrath, Fludd) but mostly as table headings or of the Stone (i=220 Khunrath calls the Stone, not man, the microcosm); Fludd i=1081/1101 apply it to the human body. No islamic passage found (lexical greps for small world / microcosm returned nothing). i=11826 (preceding Manilius page) also has the parallel world-elements / human-constitution lines.

queries.query: the divine is beyond every name and description

passages.title: Commentaries on the Mystical Theology of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite
passages.quote: concerning Him, nor name, nor knowledge. He is neither darkness nor light, neither error nor truth.
passages.why: Dionysius, Mystical Theology ch. 5: there is no discourse, name or knowledge of God; he is beyond every affirmation and negation.

passages.title: Pseudo-Dionysius Areopagita Schriften (German 1823)
passages.quote: God is nothing of that which man can see, feel, imagine, think, or sense. His concept is an eternal negation and privation
passages.why: On Dionysian language: God is named only by alpha-privatives and hyper-compounds because he exceeds everything thinkable.

passages.title: Commentaries on the Mystical Theology of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite
passages.quote: Lastly, he concludes that there is no word or knowledge of GOD: because He is above every affirmation
passages.why: Eck's commentary on Mystical Theology: no word or knowledge of God, who is above all affirmation and denial.

passages.title: On the Wonder-Working Word
passages.quote: For we express God by nothing more certainly than by a privative particle or a negative word
passages.why: Reuchlin: God is most truly expressed by negation; in his substance he is subject to no name, and affirmations state only what surrounds his nature.

passages.title: On the Art of the Kabbalah
passages.quote: let no one think that when we name gods, they are equal to the supreme and ineffable God who has no name
passages.why: Reuchlin's Kabbalist: the supreme God is ineffable and nameless, nowhere yet everywhere, more interior to each thing than itself.

passages.title: Henrici Cornelii Agrippae de nobilitate & praecellentia foeminei, sexus, ad Margaretam Augustam Austriaco. & Burgundionus principes
passages.quote: He is beyond all speech, beyond every position and abstraction, beyond every affirmation and negation
passages.why: Agrippa: reason works from the senses, but God is above all natures, numbers and orders, beyond all speech (citing Dionysius).

passages.title: On the Mysteries
passages.quote: Concerning the absolute first principle, the Egyptians said nothing, but as sōth a term for the unknown , "they praised it as unknown," says Damascius
passages.why: Notes to Iamblichus via Damascius: the first principle is beyond all understanding, praised as unknown and passed over in silence (Egyptians, Orphics).

passages.title: Taoist Texts: Ethical, Political, and Speculative
passages.quote: though it has no name, it produces the growth and nurture of all things. As I do not know its name, I am compelled to call it simply Tao
passages.why: Qingjing jing: the Tao has no form, passions or name; 'Tao' is only a forced designation.

passages.title: 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 4
passages.quote: The Way does not make them private, and therefore it is nameless. Because it is nameless, there is nothing it does not do.
passages.why: Zhuangzi (Zeyang) with commentary: the Way embraces the differing principles of all things and so is nameless.

passages.title: The Religion of the Samurai: A Study of Zen Philosophy
passages.quote: Thus, Buddha is unnamable, indescribable, and indefinable, but we provisionally call Him Buddha.
passages.why: Zen: the object of worship cannot be named or pictured; masters answer 'What is Buddha?' with silence; the name is provisional.

passages.title: The Bhagvat-Geeta, or Dialogues of Kreeshna and Arjoon
passages.quote: and invisible form—which is omnipresent, incomprehensible, exalted, fixed, and immovable
passages.why: Gita 12: Krishna's ineffable, invisible, incomprehensible nature and the harder path of those who worship it.

passages.title: Three Theological Treatises
passages.quote: and that He is not a body, nor is He like other bodies. As for establishing an existent in one's belief based on what we mentioned regarding the extreme exaggeration of sanctification
passages.why: Ghazali: 'Nothing is like Him'; God is no body nor like bodies, and pure negation of all description is too hard for most believers.

queries.reader_notes: Christian (three Dionysius volumes, i=7994-8033, 8274-8313, 8354-8393) is the core; many more pages there qualify. Reuchlin (shelved jewish-kabbalistic) is Christian Kabbalah speaking in a Jewish/Pythagorean voice. Greek evidence is second-hand (Gale's notes citing Damascius); the Proclus Platonic Theology window did not surface a clean apophatic page by grep. Islamic i=2979 is about tanzih vs anthropomorphism - weakest fit. Hindu neti-neti not in pool; Gita 12 is the nearest.

queries.query: light as the nature of the divine or of the mind

passages.title: ’chi med ’phags ma’i snying thig skor
passages.quote: Rest in the state of the great self-arisen clear light, the union of appearance and awareness.
passages.why: Introduction to the nature of mind: appearances are like reflections in a mirror arising from one's own empty mind, which is self-arisen clear light.

passages.quote: It is the light of lights, and it is declared to be free from darkness. It is wisdom itself, the object of wisdom

passages.title: Theologumena Arithmeticae (de Falco, Teubner)

passages.title: Essence of Pomegranates

passages.title: The Noble Eightfold Path: The Doctrine of Dharma
passages.quote: the spirit is born into the physical world and dies out of the physical world about eight hundred times
passages.why: Lives as school-days separated by nights of rest; reincarnation explains unequal births

passages.title: Compendium of the Five Lamps
passages.quote: those five hundred disciples, due to their meager merit and thin virtue, were reborn into the feathered race
passages.why: Chan lamp record: disciples reborn as cranes through karma, the master through many rebirths

passages.title: Initiation and Its Results

queries.query: the elements and how they change into one another

queries.query: dreams as a source of knowledge or revelation

passages.why: al-Farabi: the Active Intellect informs the imagination in sleep, yielding true dreams of particulars and divination of divine things

passages.title: Sahih al-Bukhari (Complete)

passages.why: Bukhari: the Prophet's heart does not sleep; prophets' dreams are revelation (Abraham's dream)

passages.title: The Quran
passages.quote: O eminent ones! Explain to me my vision, 44. if you are able to interpret visions.
passages.why: Quran, Sura Joseph: the king's dream of the seven cows and Joseph's God-given interpretation of dreams

passages.title: Summa Theologica
passages.quote: is diversified first according to the difference of a dream, which occurs while sleeping, and a vision, which occurs while waking, which pertains to a higher degree of prophecy
passages.why: Aquinas: degrees of prophecy; supernatural truth shown in a dream ranks below a waking vision

passages.title: Summa Theologica
passages.quote: But in sleeping, some naturally foresee certain future events, as is evident through the Philosopher

passages.title: Gates of Righteousness

passages.why: Gikatilla: prophets receive vision or dream through the partitions, in parables; only Moses saw without mediation

passages.title: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ
passages.quote: A dream is the meeting of minds; an event in our waking consciousness is the coming together of sensible substances.
passages.why: Liezi: what a dream is; those who put faith in dreams misunderstand; the pure men of old slept without dreams

passages.title: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ
passages.quote: Now I have found the deer, so it appears that his dream was a true dream.
passages.why: Liezi's deer parable: no one can tell which was the true dream and which the waking fact

passages.title: The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer
passages.quote: Whence it is that many philosophers were of opinion, that air is the cause of dreams, and of many other impressions of the mind
passages.why: Barrett's Magus (after Agrippa): the air carries the species of all things into sleepers and is the matter of dreams and divinations

passages.title: Description of Greece
passages.quote: In it, those sleeping foresee future events: for the goddess declares what is necessary through the visions of dreams.
passages.why: Pausanias: the dream-oracle of Ino at Thalamae, where sleepers learn the future from the goddess

passages.title: Bla ma dgongs 'dus skor
passages.quote: I write the hidden prophecy entrusted by the Dakini. On the 6th day of the month, In a moment when my vision became dizzy
passages.why: Tibetan treasure text: a 'Prophetic Dream-Letter' in which the dakini's prophecy and teaching are received in a visionary dream

passages.title: Compendium of the Five Lamps
passages.quote: who interpreted the dream for him, saying: "The mountain of jewels is my own body. The gushing spring represents the inexhaustible Dharma.
passages.why: Chan lamp record: a father's dream at the patriarch's birth is read as foretelling his entry into the Dharma

queries.reader_notes: Hindu-indic: dream appears only as a state of consciousness (waking/dream/deep sleep) or as a simile for unreality, never as a source of knowledge in the pool; Panchatantra i=7428 has a narrative dream-vision only. queries.query: what happens to the soul after death; judgment of the dead

passages.title: The Republic
passages.quote: He saw then, in this way, the souls departing through each opening of both heaven and earth after they had been judged
passages.why: Plato, myth of Er: judges sit between the openings and send the just upward and the unjust downward

passages.title: The Republic
passages.quote: for all the wrongs they had committed and for all the people they had wronged, they paid the penalty for each in turn, tenfold for each
passages.why: Plato, myth of Er: tenfold punishment and reward of souls over a thousand years

passages.title: The Republic
passages.quote: are nothing in number or size compared to those things which await each man after death.
passages.why: Plato: the rewards of justice in life are nothing beside what awaits after death; introduces the vision of Er

passages.title: Complete Text of the Quran (Alcorani Textus Universus)

passages.why: Tibetan instruction: stages of dying, the clear light, the bardo states and the flight into a womb

passages.why: Taoist ethical tract (Balfour): the law of retribution follows the dead, who return as python or cow according to their crimes

queries.query: how the world first came into being

passages.quote: From water, undergoing transformation, arose the earth ( bhūta ), which possesses smell.
passages.why: Bhagavata Purana, 'The Process of Creation': from the tamasic ego arise ether, air, fire, water and earth in order

passages.title: Śrīmad Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Dvitīya Skandha) with Bhāvārtha Dīpikā
passages.quote: He, the Lord Viṣṇu , assumes māyā for the sake of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

passages.title: The Compendium of Shiva
passages.quote: The wise have thus explained the creation of the world—the tattwas

passages.title: Confucian Cosmogony
passages.quote: In this section the Primordial Air is treated of as divided into two Airs, in order to the formation of the complete Kosmos

passages.title: Confucian Cosmogony
passages.quote: When Heaven and Earth create living things, the Five Elements are the very first to appear.
passages.why: Zhu Xi: yang transforms and yin combines, generating the Five Phases, the first things to appear when heaven and earth produce beings

passages.title: Two Books Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World
passages.quote: For this cause, and from these four things, the body of the world was created, constructed by the proportion I have described.
passages.why: Philoponus quoting Plato's Timaeus: God joined fire, air, water and earth by proportion to make the body of the world

passages.title: Two Books Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World
passages.quote: For Plato openly asserts that the world was produced from a certain beginning, that it does not always exist, and that it did not exist before it was created.
passages.why: Philoponus against Proclus: Plato taught that the world had a beginning and was made, not eternal

passages.title: On the Nature and Origin of the Doctrine of Emanation among the Kabbalists

passages.title: On the Hyleal Chaos
passages.quote: entering into the Hyleal, that is, Pri-material watery CHAOS created at the first beginning of the World, sanctifying and also impregnating it
passages.why: Khunrath: divine light and fire enter and impregnate the primal material chaos from which the great world is built

passages.title: Die Philosophie der Alten wiederkommend in der güldenen Zeit : worinnen von den unsichtbaren Anfängen des spiritus rectoris oder bildenden Geists in den Pflanzen ... gehandelt wird

left_out.query: controlling the breath as a spiritual practice

passages.quote: and let the nasal breathing gradually cease. If the breath becomes hurried, swallow it slowly.
passages.why: Daoist inner cultivation: still the mind, circulate qi through the two vessels, swallow breath down to the cinnabar field, let nasal breathing cease.

passages.title: Declarations of the Perfected
passages.quote: Always at dawn, face the sun, inhale the air, and swallow it. This is called Na rijing Absorbing the Essence of the Sun .

passages.title: Thadrak Thor bu 034 Zab don rnam bshad snying po

passages.title: Compendium of the Five Lamps
passages.quote: when breathing out, does not follow worldly conditions; when breathing in, does not dwell in the realms of the five aggregates
